title: Play Is How Young Children Learn
hook: For young children, play isn't a break from learning — it is the learning, building language, problem-solving, and social skills all at once.
key_points: Unstructured, child-led play develops imagination, planning, and the ability to negotiate with others.
Pretend play lets children rehearse real-world roles and practice managing emotions.
Simple, open-ended materials (blocks, boxes, dress-up) often spark richer play than single-purpose toys.
Adults help most by joining in and following the child's lead, not by directing every step.
content_html: It's easy to see play as the fun stuff that happens around the real work of learning. For young children, that's backwards: play is the primary way they learn. A child stacking blocks is testing physics; one playing make-believe is rehearsing language, social roles, and emotional regulation all at once.
extra_html: Open-ended materials — blocks, cardboard boxes, dress-up clothes — often spark richer play than toys that do only one thing, because the child has to supply the imagination. And adults help most not by directing the play but by joining in and following the child's lead, adding a question or a new idea when invited. The American Academy of Pediatrics frames play as "brain building" — central to healthy development, not a break from it; your pediatrician can suggest play ideas suited to your child.

related.title: What School Readiness Really Means
related.hook: Being ready for school is less about reading early and more about social and emotional skills — following directions, taking turns, and managing feelings.

related.title: The Toddler Language Explosion
related.hook: Somewhere in the second year, many toddlers go from a handful of words to picking up new ones almost daily — and talking with them is what fuels it.

related.title: Why Outdoor Play Punches Above Its Weight
related.hook: Time outside does more than burn energy. It builds strong bodies, sharper focus, braver problem-solvers — and a growing body of research links it to healthier eyesight.

flashcards.prompt: What kinds of toys tend to spark the richest play?

choices.text: Simple, open-ended materials like blocks and boxes
Single-purpose electronic toys that do one thing
Only the newest, most expensive toys

flashcards.explanation_html: Open-ended materials let children invent and direct their own play, which builds imagination, planning, and problem-solving.

flashcards.prompt: How can an adult best support a young child's play?
flashcards.back_html: By joining in and following the child's lead rather than directing every step — child-led play does the developmental heavy lifting.
